lessons.title: Order Book Imbalance as a Short-Horizon Alpha Signal

body.text: Order book imbalance does not need a sequence of updates the way order flow imbalance does, a single snapshot of resting bid and ask quantity is enough to lean a fair-value estimate away from the plain midpoint and toward where price is more likely to move next.

children.text: A Simpler, State-Based Cousin of OFI

Order flow imbalance from Chapter 3 is a flow measure: it needs consecutive book updates to compute, since it is built entirely from how the book changed. Order book imbalance, OBI, is different and simpler, it is a state measure, computable from a single snapshot, comparing the quantity resting on the bid side against the quantity resting on the ask side right now.

body.caption: Order book imbalance ranges from -1, all visible liquidity on the ask side, to +1, all visible liquidity on the bid side. V can be the best-level quantity alone or summed across several depth levels.

children.text: Sasha Stoikov's 2018 paper, "The Micro-Price: A High-Frequency Estimator of Future Prices," turns OBI into a genuinely useful fair-value estimate. Instead of treating the plain midpoint from Chapter 1 as the best available reference price, the microprice weights the bid and ask by each other's quantity, so that a heavily imbalanced book pulls the estimate meaningfully off the midpoint and toward wherever price is more likely to move next.

body.caption: The microprice. Notice the weights are swapped: the bid price is weighted by the ask quantity, and the ask price by the bid quantity, so a large bid quantity pulls the estimate toward the ask price, not the bid.

children.text: That swapped weighting is the entire idea, and it is easy to misread at first. A large resting bid quantity relative to the ask means there is more buying interest queued up than selling interest, which historically tends to precede price moving up toward and through the ask, so the microprice leans toward the ask price to reflect that, not toward the bid.

body.caption: Two snapshots of the same stock, opposite imbalance
Reproducing the table above exactly. Notice the two snapshots share the identical midpoint but the microprice diverges from it in opposite directions.

children.text: This is not just an ad hoc reweighting. Earlier work on order book dynamics, including Cont, Stoikov, and Talreja's 2010 stochastic model of the limit order book, showed the probability that the next price tick is up rather than down moves monotonically with the current order book imbalance, more resting buy interest relative to sell interest genuinely does raise the odds of an upward tick over very short horizons. The intuition connects directly to price-time priority from Chapter 2: a deep resting bid means there is a large queue of buy orders ready to absorb selling pressure without price falling, while a thin ask means comparatively little resting supply stands between the current price and the next level up.

The formula above works with just the best bid and ask, Level 1 OBI, which reacts fastest but can be noisy, a single large or small order at the touch can swing it sharply. Summing quantity across several depth levels, using the full five-level snapshots from Chapter 1, produces a steadier Multi-Level OBI that reflects more of the book's genuine structure at the cost of reacting slightly slower to change. Which one to use depends on the horizon a signal is targeting, a strategy holding for a few seconds cares mostly about Level 1, while one holding for a few minutes benefits from the steadier multi-level version.

body.title: Order Book Imbalance vs Order Flow Imbalance

columns.label: Order Book Imbalance (This Lesson)
points: A state measure, computed from a single current snapshot
Simple ratio of resting bid quantity to ask quantity
Directly produces the microprice, an improved fair-value estimate
Very fast to compute, well suited to the shortest horizons

columns.label: Order Flow Imbalance (Chapter 3)
points: A flow measure, computed from a sequence of consecutive updates
Tracks how the book's own composition is changing, not just its current state
Captures information from cancellations, not only resting size
Better suited to detecting building pressure over a longer buildup, as in the Chapter 3 case study

body.text: Order book imbalance can be manipulated. A trader can place a large resting order with no genuine intention of letting it fill, purely to bias OBI and the microprice, then cancel it moments later. This kind of spoofing is market manipulation, illegal on NSE and BSE under SEBI regulations and actively monitored by exchange surveillance, and it is also a real practical risk: a naive signal reading raw OBI without any regard for how quickly resting size tends to appear and vanish can be fooled by exactly this pattern.

body.title: Computing a Microprice
body.prompt: The best bid for a stock is ₹640.00 with 1,500 shares resting, and the best ask is ₹640.10 with 4,500 shares resting. What is the microprice?
body.explanation: Microprice = P_bid × (V_ask / total) + P_ask × (V_bid / total) = 640.00 × (4,500 / 6,000) + 640.10 × (1,500 / 6,000) = 640.00 × 0.75 + 640.10 × 0.25 = 480.00 + 160.025 = 640.025. The plain midpoint here is ₹640.05, so the microprice sits below it, leaning toward the bid, correctly reflecting that the ask side is far more heavily supplied than the bid side in this snapshot.

body.title: Reading a Suspicious OBI Spike
body.question: A trader notices order book imbalance on a stock suddenly turn strongly positive after a single very large resting bid appears, and then watches that same bid get cancelled moments later without ever trading. What does this illustrate about using raw OBI as a signal?
options: OBI is always a completely reliable signal regardless of how the underlying orders behave
Large resting orders can be placed with no genuine intention of being filled, which can bias OBI without reflecting real buying interest
This pattern proves the stock is about to rally, since OBI briefly turned strongly positive
OBI cannot be manipulated because it is computed directly from exchange data
body.explanation: Raw resting quantity says nothing about the intent behind an order. A large bid placed and cancelled without trading is a textbook spoofing pattern, and it can move OBI and the microprice just as much as genuine buying interest would, which is exactly why any real signal built on OBI needs some way to account for how persistent resting size actually is, not just how large it looks in a single snapshot.

points: Order book imbalance is a state-based signal computed from a single snapshot, unlike order flow imbalance's sequence of updates from Chapter 3
OBI = (bid quantity minus ask quantity) divided by their sum, ranging from -1 to +1
The microprice reweights the bid and ask by the opposite side's quantity, pulling the fair-value estimate away from the plain midpoint and toward the side more likely to be reached next
Academic work on limit order book dynamics has shown the probability of the next price tick moving up rises monotonically with order book imbalance
Level 1 OBI reacts fastest but is noisiest; multi-level OBI is steadier but slower to react, and the right choice depends on a signal's target horizon
OBI can be manipulated through spoofing, large orders placed and cancelled without genuine intent to trade, which any real signal needs to account for rather than trusting raw resting size alone
